title: Stage 7: 50M users
scopeHtml: Scope: search with Elasticsearch, media pipeline, rate limiting, API gateway, when to split services and when not to. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Load and goal
notes.html:
Stage 7 goal: Chirp reaches 50M registered users and gains the features users expect from a real platform: search, image/video posts, protection from abusive clients, and a team structure that no longer fits one codebase. The question is not just "what to add" but "what to leave alone".

Quantity Value Derivation
Registered / DAU 50M / 20M 40% DAU
Posts 10M/day = 116/s avg, 350/s peak 0.5 per DAU
Posts with media 25% = 2.5M/day = 29/s avg
Average image after resize set 4 variants totalling about 600 KB thumb, small, medium, original
Media storage growth 2.5M x 600 KB = 1.5 TB/day, 550 TB/year
Search queries 20M DAU x 1 = 20M/day = 230/s avg, 700/s peak
Timeline reads 400M/day = 4,600/s avg, 14k/s peak
Engineers about 80 in 10 teams

Industry examples. Twitter's early search was Lucene-based "Earlybird" over in-memory recent index; Instagram runs Django still as the core monolith at a very large scale, extracting only specific services; Shopify famously stayed a "modular monolith".

Everyday analogy. A town grows: you add a library (search), a warehouse (media), a security gate (rate limit) and a few town departments, but you do not break every room into its own building.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating search as "add an index to SQL". Full text, ranking and typo tolerance need a real search engine.
  • Splitting into microservices because the company is "big now".

notes.title: Configuration
notes.html:
Search (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch).

Setting Value
Index time-based: posts-2026.11 monthly, plus rollover at 50 GB per shard
Data volume 10M posts/day x 1 KB indexed = 10 GB/day, 300 GB/month, replicas x2
Cluster 3 dedicated masters m6g.large, 6 data nodes r6g.2xlarge (64 GB RAM, 1.5 TB gp3)
Shards 6 primaries per monthly index, 1 replica each; target shard size 20 to 50 GB
Heap 31 GB or less (stay under compressed-oops limit), rest left to OS page cache
Refresh interval 5s (near real time; 1s is costly)
Hot/warm indexes older than 30 days go to warm nodes, older than 12 months to cheap storage or closed 
{
  "settings": { "number_of_shards": 6, "number_of_replicas": 1, "refresh_interval": "5s" },
  "mappings": { "properties": {
    "text": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "standard" },
    "author_id": { "type": "keyword" },
    "created_at": { "type": "date" },
    "lang": { "type": "keyword" },
    "like_count": { "type": "integer" }
  } }
}

Media pipeline.

  • Presigned URL TTL 10 min, max size 5 MB image / 512 MB video.
  • Resize workers: 20 x c6i.2xlarge consuming SQS, visibility timeout 120 s, dead-letter queue after 5 receives. Output WebP/AVIF at 150, 480, 1080 px; videos transcoded by a managed service (for example AWS MediaConvert) into HLS ladders.
  • CDN: cache images 1 year (Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable) with content-hash URLs.

Rate limiting at the gateway.

Limit Value
Per user, write posts 300/hour
Per user, reads 900 per 15 min on timeline
Per IP unauthenticated 60/min
Algorithm token bucket in Redis, Lua script, key rl:{user}:{route}
Redis dedicated 3-shard cluster cache.r6g.large

API gateway. Envoy or Kong, 8 pods, handles TLS termination, JWT validation, rate limit, request ids, routing. Timeouts: connect 1 s, request 5 s, retries 1 on idempotent GET only.

Common interview traps.

  • Giving Elasticsearch 64 GB heap; it breaks compressed pointers and starves the page cache.
  • Uploading media through your API servers instead of presigned URLs.
  • Retrying non-idempotent POSTs at the gateway.

notes.title: Decision and why
notes.html:
1. Search: Elasticsearch fed by Kafka (change data), not Postgres full text. Postgres tsvector is fine to about a few million rows, but we have 3.6B posts per year spread over 16 shards. A search needs a scatter-gather and ranking. Elasticsearch gives inverted indexes, BM25 ranking, language analyzers, faceting. The index is a derived copy: Postgres stays the source of truth. A consumer reads post.created, post.deleted from Kafka and writes to the index. Expect indexing lag of 5 to 10 s; "search is eventually consistent" is acceptable, but deletes must propagate within minutes for legal reasons.

2. Media: store blobs in object storage, never in the DB, and process asynchronously. Upload cost is bandwidth and CPU for resizing; neither belongs in the request thread. Original is kept (reprocess later when a new format arrives), variants are served from CDN. At 550 TB/year storage on S3 Standard-IA after 30 days costs about $0.0125/GB-month, so lifecycle rules matter.

3. Rate limiting at the edge using token bucket. Allows bursts (bucket size 30) yet bounds average rate (refill 5/s). Protects the databases from scripts; also a basic abuse control.

4. When to split services. Split only when at least one holds:

  • A part has a very different scaling profile (media processing is CPU and bursty; search is memory heavy).
  • A part has different reliability needs (notifications must not take down posting).
  • A team boundary exists with an independent release cadence and clear API.
  • A part uses a different runtime (Python ML ranking, ffmpeg).

Chirp extracts: media-processor, search-indexer/query, notification-sender, fan-out workers (already). The core (users, posts, timeline read, follow graph) stays a modular monolith with enforced package boundaries.

When NOT to split. When the pieces share a transaction (post plus counter plus timeline entry), when the team is small enough to coordinate in a chat room, when the only argument is "it is cleaner". Each service split adds a network hop (1 to 5 ms), a failure mode, a deploy pipeline and distributed tracing needs. Amazon Prime Video's 2023 move of a monitoring pipeline from microservices back to a monolith cut cost about 90%, a well-known cautionary tale.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual-writing to DB and Elasticsearch in the request path; if one fails you are inconsistent. Use an outbox plus Kafka.
  • Saying "microservices" as the answer to scale. Scale is solved by stateless replication; services solve team and failure isolation.

notes.title: Alternatives (branches)
notes.html:
Branch A: How to feed search

Dual write in app Outbox/CDC to Kafka Batch reindex
Consistency can drift on partial failure at-least-once, replayable stale up to 24 h
Latency to searchable immediate 5 to 10 s hours
Complexity low medium (Debezium, Kafka) low
Recovery manual replay offset rerun

Choose outbox/CDC. Replaying the topic lets you rebuild the index after a mapping change.

Branch B: Search technology

Postgres FTS Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Algolia/managed Custom Lucene
Ops cost none high none very high
Scale millions of docs billions depends on price billions
Features basic rich rich whatever you build
Per-request cost in your DB cluster per-search fee cluster

Choose Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, possibly managed (Amazon OpenSearch Service). At 230 queries/s a managed SaaS billed per query becomes more expensive than owning 6 nodes.

Branch C: Monolith vs microservices vs modular monolith

Monolith Modular monolith + few services Microservices
Deploy independence none partial full
Latency in-process mostly in-process many network hops
Team scaling up to about 30 30 to 150 100+
Ops overhead low medium high (mesh, tracing, per-service CI)

Choose modular monolith + 4 extracted services at 80 engineers. Revisit at about 200 engineers or when a module's deploy cadence blocks others.

Branch D: Rate limit algorithm

Algorithm Behaviour Memory Notes
Fixed window simple, double burst at window edge 1 counter cheap
Sliding log exact O(requests) expensive
Sliding window counter approx. exact 2 counters good compromise
Token bucket allows bursts, bounded average 2 fields most used (Stripe, AWS)

Choose token bucket with an atomic Lua script. Local in-gateway buckets with periodic sync are an option if Redis latency (0.5 ms) matters, trading accuracy.

Common interview traps.

  • Not discussing what happens if the rate-limit Redis is down. Choose fail-open for reads, fail-closed for sensitive endpoints such as login.
  • Using IP alone behind NAT; a university campus shares one IP.

notes.title: What breaks next
notes.html:
1. Elasticsearch hot shards: a trending hashtag sends 40% of queries to the newest index. Fix with request cache, query result TTL 10 s, and more replicas on the hot index.
  2. Cluster state bloat when you create too many tiny indexes: keep shard count in the low thousands per cluster.
  3. Single data centre failure. All of this is in one AZ or a poorly balanced pair; Stage 8 addresses availability.
  4. Cascading failure: search slow, API threads wait, whole site slows. Needs timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads (Stage 8).
  5. Poison media: a corrupt 500 MB video loops in the worker; DLQ and max-attempts rule.
  6. Deploy blast radius: one monolith build touches everything; canary and feature flags needed.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a replica makes you highly available. Replicas in the same AZ do not survive an AZ loss.

notes.title: Cost
notes.html:
Delta over Stage 6 (monthly, approximate; Stage 6 baseline scaled to 50M is also larger).

Item Monthly
Elasticsearch: 6 x r6g.2xlarge at about $480 + 3 masters + storage $4,500
S3 media: 1.5 TB/day grows; steady-state first year average 270 TB at blended $0.018/GB $5,000, grows $200 per day-of-new-data
Resize workers 20 x c6i.2xlarge $5,000 (use spot to cut 60%)
CDN egress: say 800 TB/month at about $0.03/GB blended $24,000
Gateway 8 pods + rate limit Redis $1,800
Scaled core (API 40 nodes, posts 8 hosts, Redis 36 nodes) about $85,000
Total about $125,000/month, $2.5 per 1,000 registered users

CDN egress is the surprise line item; compress, use AVIF, negotiate committed-use pricing.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting egress. Media-heavy apps are CDN-cost bound.
  • Not using spot or preemptible instances for stateless batch workers.

notes.title: LLD view
notes.html:
interface MediaStore {
    UploadTicket presign(UserId u, MediaType t, long size);   // returns URL, expires 10 min
}

class MediaWorker {
    void handle(S3Event e) {
        Image img = download(e.key());
        for (int w : new int[]{150, 480, 1080}) {
            upload(e.key() + "_" + w + ".webp", resize(img, w));
        }
        markReady(e.key());           // idempotent: sets status READY if not already
    }
}

class TokenBucket {  // conceptually; production is a Lua script
    boolean allow(String key, int cap, double refillPerSec, long nowMs) { /* ... */ return true; }
}
# Redis Lua script outline for token bucket (one atomic call)
# KEYS[1]=bucket  ARGV: capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms
# tokens, ts = HMGET bucket; refill = min(cap, tokens + (now-ts)*rate)
# if refill >= 1: store refill-1, return 1 else store refill, return 0

Modular boundaries. Packages users, posts, timeline, graph, notify each expose an interface; others may call only the interface. Enforce with ArchUnit or module visibility so later extraction is cheap.

Common interview traps.

  • Cross-module database joins; they make later extraction impossible.
  • Processing the same media twice after a redelivery; keep the handler idempotent.

notes.title: Decision gravity
notes.html:
Decision Gravity Why
Elasticsearch as derived index Reversible Rebuild from Kafka or DB; can switch engines
Outbox pattern Reversible Additive
Object storage for media with content-hash keys Mostly one-way URLs are baked into posts, caches and clients
Presigned direct uploads Reversible Client protocol, versioned
Rate limits (values) Reversible Config
Extracting a service One-way-ish Easy to extract, expensive to merge back; data ownership moves
API gateway as the single entry Reversible but sticky Everything depends on it

Rule of thumb: derive data, keep source in one place; extract a service only when the pain is measured.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating a service split as free. It is a long-lived contract.

notes.title: Concepts learned
notes.html:
• Inverted index, BM25, shards and replicas, hot/warm tiers
  • Outbox pattern, CDC, at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers
  • Presigned URLs, async media pipelines, dead-letter queues
  • Token bucket and other rate limiting algorithms; fail-open vs fail-closed
  • API gateway responsibilities
  • Modular monolith; criteria for splitting a service and for not splitting

Common interview traps.

  • Using "microservices" without naming which criterion justified each service.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• At 50M users add search (Elasticsearch fed by outbox plus Kafka, 6 data nodes), a media pipeline (presigned upload, async resize, CDN with immutable URLs), edge rate limiting (token bucket in Redis) and a gateway.
  • Keep Postgres the source of truth; search and timelines are derived and rebuildable.
  • Split services by scaling profile, reliability needs, team boundary or runtime; otherwise stay a modular monolith.
  • Cost is about $125k/month and CDN egress dominates.
  • Next risk: cascading failure and single-AZ loss, which Stage 8 handles.
